correctness.rationale: An exact boundary decomposition gives the two first variations \(\partial_a E_p=4a^pG_p(b/a)\) and \(\partial_b E_p=4b^pG_p(a/b)\). The normalized derivative is \(G_p^{\prime}(r)=p(1+r)(1+r^2)^{p/2-1}\); integration by parts gives \(G_p(1)=(p+1)\int_0^1(1+t^2)^{p/2}\,dt>0\), while the limit at infinity is negative for \(-1<p<0\). Hence exactly one root lies above one. The valid half-side parameter wedge is convex. Its gradient is componentwise nonnegative and never both zero, so integration along any positive inclusion displacement proves strict global monotonicity. Outside the wedge, a negative short-side derivative yields actual nearby counterexamples. The remaining exponent cases follow from positivity, the explicit boundary-exponent formula and homogeneity. Implicit differentiation proves the critical ratio strictly increasing, implicit-function expansion gives the lower-endpoint slope, and dominated convergence gives the upper-endpoint limit. The analytic proof covers the full parameter domain; 902 numerical checks only supplement it.

originality.rationale: The exact sharp negative-power inclusion monotonicity wedge for centered rectangles, its inverse critical-exponent curve, and both endpoint laws were not obtained from the compared sources. The closest papers concern fixed-unweighted-perimeter shape optimization, the sufficient hypothesis of increasing radial weights for unrestricted convex bodies, or global rigidity for every inclusion pair. Their theorems do not imply positive monotonicity for a decreasing singular weight in a restricted eccentricity family. These distinctions are based on mathematical statements and inspected material, not title similarity. Priority remains provisional.

value.rationale: The recent weighted-perimeter literature establishes unrestricted inclusion monotonicity for increasing radial densities and shows negative-power weights do not enjoy unrestricted monotonicity. It is mathematically natural to ask for the largest anisotropy class of centered rectangles where negative-power monotonicity remains valid. The finding completely classifies it, locates a sharp continuous critical aspect/exponent curve, proves global (not merely differential) positive comparison, gives sharp reverse inclusions beyond the boundary, and determines singular endpoint laws. The exact cutoffs are therefore motivated natural geometric invariants, not arbitrary computational slices; general convex-body extensions are not claimed.
